utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Once again, I warn you, Witness, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was just rising to continue my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. As I said yesterday, I'm almost finished.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I continue with the questions I was asking yesterday, I wanted to go back just for a moment and ask you a question about the police station in Drnis in August of 1990. You testified that, and I'm quoting: "As far as I know, even though I'm not all that familiar with that because I didn't actually work there, but as far as I know the ratio between Serb and Croat policemen was more or less equal." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you accept the possibility that, in fact, there were -- that the police station was predominantly Serb and that there was a minority number of Croat policemen there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, esteemed Prosecutor, I would accept that if there was a document indicating what you have just explained. Things being what they are, I have to abide by my previous position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, no, I wasn't actually asking that. What -- I was trying to get a feel for how sure you are about this fact, because in your testimony you said: "I'm not all that familiar with that because I didn't actually work there." So I'm trying to put to you whether you would accept the possibility that there were more -- many more Serbs than Croats, in fact, in that police department.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that possibility. I used to know the previous chief there. We were on good terms. We would spend sometime talking and we talked about this too. Later on, employees, officers, who arrived at that station from Knin were speaking about a 50/50 ratio in terms of the ethnic distribution, and that is where I get my information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You described in your testimony the insignia, the patch, that the SAO Krajina police began to wear around the summer of 1991, and you described it as "a semi-circular lettering saying 'Milicija,' police, and then 'Milicija of Krajina,' Krajina Police, and then in the middle there was the tri-coloured flag." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure about the interpretation I have just received. I said there was a semi-circular lettering saying "Milicija" and then just underneath it said "Krajina." Above the "Milicija" word and underneath the "Krajina" word was a tri-coloured flag, meaning the word "Milicija" appears just once and the word "Krajina" just underneath likewise appears once only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand. Just to be clear, the tri-coloured flag is above "Krajina" and below "Milicija"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could see we Exhibit 266, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this the patch that you were describing, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I want to go back to Benkovac in 1992. When you were in Benkovac, were you familiar with two officers by the name of Milan Veselinovic and Jovo Zecevic? Are you familiar with those two officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, these men were not officers. As far as I know, they were erstwhile members of the police, but later they became members of a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Whether I used the word "officers," I'm thinking of members of the police, but I understand that the translation may suggest something different. So in August of 1992, what was the status of these two men? Were they members of the police at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, they were members of special police units, the Krajina border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were they within the Benkovac public security station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time. They fell under the jurisdiction of the Knin SUP. These were police forces that covered the borders. The public security station is a lower level unit in terms of organisation, and public security stations did not control the borders. The borders were under the Knin SUP. There was a special department coordinating the work of all these minor units, patrolling the borders. We at Benkovac sometimes provided logistics for them, but we did not coordinate their work and they were not under our command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about a special unit that was in Benkovac that had, among other things, a military function. That special unit, did that fall under the command of the Benkovac public security station or did that fall under the command of the Knin SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this unit was about 25 or 26 men strong. It was called the Benkovac special police unit. Establishment-wise it belonged to the Benkovac public security station, but during war operations, it would join other units from throughout Dalmatia in order to form a company and then it would place itself under the command of a military unit. Usually at the front line military commanders were in charge and the police commanders were normally in charge further back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the two men who I mentioned, Milan Veselinovic and Jovo Zecevic, were they members of the Benkovac special police unit or were they members some other special police unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two police officers you've mentioned were not members of the Benkovac special unit or the Benkovac station. They belonged to a department of the Knin SUP and were deployed at the border crossing called Stabanj, which is on the way from Benkovac towards Biograd at the far end. There was a border crossing and their task was to patrol or control that border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 3rd of August, 1992, these two policemen arrested a Croat by the name of Davor Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with that occurrence at the time, but now that you've mentioned it, this had something to do with me. Back in 2000 I received an Interpol arrest warrant indicating that I, too, had been involved in this arrest so I became interested, naturally. I can explain, time allowing. It was not until after the war, back in 2001, that I became, to some extent, familiar with this case you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me try and ask you some questions and we'll see if I can get your evidence on this issue. The arrest warrant that implicated you, did you become aware that at some point that was withdrawn or dismissed against you? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned later that the arrest warrant against me and two other men had been withdrawn. As for these other two people, Zecevic and Milan Veselinovic, the arrest warrant against them was still in force but I only learned about this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you did not know -- hear anything about this in 1992, about this -- what happened to Davor Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in 1992, I was not familiar with any of the details. It wasn't before the year 2000 that I found out about a number of details. As for Davor Lukic, he is one of the 13 cases that I discussed in the first days. People who made an illegal crossing into the Krajina area, these people were arrested and after a while returned untouched to Croat-controlled territory. This is one of the 13 illegal border crossings that I mentioned. I'm sure that this man you just mentioned, Davor Lukic, was one of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, since you say that he was returned untouched, let me just put to you what is derived from his own statement on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness didn't say that nothing happened to them. He said one of the 13 cases who were returned alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see "alive." I see here: "This is one of the 13 illegal borders crossings that I mentioned. I'm sure that this man you just mentioned, Davor Lukic, was one of these people." I don't know where you get "alive" from, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the witness's language and I know what he said. He said, "One of the 13 cases who were returned alive." That's what he said. And that was his testimony during examination-in-chief, and the interpretation here does not contain the word "alive."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then that's what you must say. Tell us that the interpretation is incorrect and stop threatening me, okay? Because it does say here: "These people were arrested and after a while returned untouched to Croat-controlled territory." Now, are you saying that "untouched" should mean "alive," were returned alive, to Croat territory? We can put it that way, which would mean, in fact, that -- which would not exclude --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can't leave it like that. My apologies, Your Honour. First of all, I apologise because I never meant to threaten anyone. It was probably my body language and that was because I was reacting to the transcript. It certainly wasn't directed at you, Your Honour. Further, I need to apologise, it was even before I had seen the transcript. I was reacting to my learned friend's the Prosecutor's question because I had just heard the sentence uttered by the witness who said this was one of the 13 cases who were returned alive. In examination-in-chief, he spoke about 13 illegal border crossings. When speaking about the document produced by Mr. McElligott, he said: "There were 13 illegal border crossings into our territory by Croats, and they were all returned alive. There was a Serb who crossed over into Croatian territory and when he returned he was mincemeat, nothing more than that, and his lung had been pierced." That is why the witness was emphasising that these 13 persons were returned alive, and I'm not myself familiar with any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can clear it up with the witness. I'm happy to clear it up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, as you've probably gathered we have a little question about the interpretation. Did you say that the -- that he returned -- that he was returned alive or untouched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you know -- did you learn at the time -- you said that you learned only details later. I'm just going to ask you and see what you might have known at the time and what you learned later. Did you learn at the time that the two officers that I mentioned, I'm sorry, two policemen that I mentioned, took Mr. Lukic to a -- after they arrested him at the border and seized him, they took him to a restaurant and tied him and kicked him all over his body and accused him of being a member of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see no foundation for this question. I see no foundation. The witness did say that it wasn't before 2000, and this was an arrest warrant issued against him, that he learned about this case. It wasn't before the year 2000 that he found out about some details that this was a person who had made an illegal border crossing, was eventually arrested and returned alive. To examine the witness now on what had become of this person who was harmed, as the Prosecutor suggests, while the witness is telling us that he's not really familiar with that, well, what that indicates to me is that there is no foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I don't know what you mean by foundation, and I think you are interrupting the cross-examination unfairly. The question -- the Prosecution says: Very well. Now, did you know -- did you learn at the time -- you said that you learned only details later. I'm just going to ask you and see what you might have known at the time and what you learned later." He's going to ask him those questions, and it is for the witness to say, now, that I didn't know at the time, this I did know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that's what the Prosecutor had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to the question. Did you learn at the time in 1992 that these two policemen took this man, Davor Lukic, to a restaurant after they arrested him, they tied him, kicked him all over his body, and accused him of being a member of a terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this happened, I wasn't aware of that case or the detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you aware that this man was -- Davor Lukic was taken to the Benkovac public security station where he was held, interrogated, and mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you not even aware that he -- that Davor Lukic was held in the public security station from the time of his arrest on the 3rd of August, 1992, until his release on the 28th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it didn't happen the way you just described it to me, because if things had happened this way, then I should have known, but I don't think he stayed in the public security station for any amount of time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know a police officer -- a policeman by the name of Djoko Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a man named Djuro Vukasinovic, also known as Djoko. He worked at the public security station and later started working with the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In August of 1992, was he working in the public security station in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was, no. In fact, he wasn't. He had already transferred to the security services of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Lukic first ended up in the barracks and then after that with the misdemeanours magistrate in Knin but certainly not in the Benkovac public security station. If you want to hear a full account, I can give it to you and then you can check that against your own information, and then after that it will be down to the Chamber to judge the veracity of all this different information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you one more question, then I'll ask you for that full account. Did you know, were Sasa and Dragan Matic policemen in the Benkovac public security station in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's not a clear answer to the question. Were they -- you say you remember that young man. First of all, I asked you about two men, Sasa and Dragan Matic, two different men. Were they both policemen in the Benkovac public security station in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my answer was somewhat imprecise because the interpretation had not yet finished. But now that you have repeated your question, I can tell you that both Sasa and Dragan Matic, two brothers, were members of the Benkovac public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, did you know anything else about this case of the arrest of Davor Lukic at the time, in 1992? What -- tell us everything that you knew, that you haven't told us so far, about the arrest of Davor Lukic in 1992, that you knew at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly tell you anything about that. I was not really familiar with that back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But were you -- were you aware that this man had been arrested? Were you even aware of that fact, simply that fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have been aware at the time, I'm not sure how, aware of an exchange of information with the army. But it's been 13 or 14 years since, and it's difficult for me to remember now whether I'd heard of something like that. I am not a native of the area myself. Thousands of persons and bits of information have filtered through my mind since, and it's difficult to remember anyone in particular. It's very difficult for me to remember all the 13 names. I can't remember the names of all the people who were killed, all those who were arrested. At least I would need to use some notes, something to jog my memory. This is an enormous amount of names and figures that need to be sorted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, following on from that answer, would it be fair to say that in -- when you were in the -- at the public security station in Benkovac in 1992, 1993, that your knowledge was really about that area, about the area around Benkovac, and that you wouldn't know the details of what was happening in areas outside of Benkovac? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't think this is a fair conclusion, not from where I stand. I was familiar with the situation throughout my area of responsibility. I wasn't aware of things that weren't within my remit but I was certainly aware of everything that was going on, things that were within my remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's actually what I meant to -- what I was trying to ask you. You were aware of what was happening within your area of responsibility; in other words, the area of responsibility of the Benkovac public security station, but not of things outside of that area of responsibility. Is that now a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know details about what happened in the military aspect or the civilian authorities' work, although I may have had bits and pieces about that too. But I'm honestly trying hard to share with this Court everything that I do know, and you can easily check through your papers whether what I am saying is consistent with what you know. But I'm trying to tell you all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get a sense of where your knowledge is and where it might not be. So I take it that public security stations in other areas of the Krajina outside of the Benkovac public security station, other public security stations, you wouldn't know the details of what was happening at those public security stations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I was partially informed, either from conversations with colleagues or joint briefings with my superiors or joint briefings within our office, such as the one we had with chiefs of civilian police in Sector South, on which occasions we shared information about some particular cases. If I was interested in a particular case, I would try to elicit more information, even if it happened in another area. There were places in Sector South where I had never set foot upon, but I still knew some things that I heard at meetings about those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your knowledge about those areas were -- would be from conversations with colleagues or these joint briefings and would generally pertain to particular cases. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, would you agree -- or let me put it this way: You would agree, wouldn't you, that by 1994, most of the Croat population in the RSK had left the RSK, by 1994? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what exactly you mean by "most of the Croat population," but quite a lot of inhabitants had left the territory of the RSK by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, I want to go back for a moment. You testified with regard to 1993 that there were -- you testified about convoys of Croat civilians out of the RSK that occurred after the attack at Maslenica in January of 1993. Are you aware that these convoys were already escorting Croat civilians out of the RSK from Vrpolje in 1992? Or do you not know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about those convoys out of Vrpolje in 1992. I told you in my prior testimony that as far as the leaving of Croats from Krajina after the aggression of the Croat army --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you've fully answered the question. You don't need to -- we have your testimony about 1993 and there is no need to repeat that, and now you've answered about Vrpolje in 1992. Sir, can you tell us the last time that you saw Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when I saw him for the last time before coming to this Tribunal, but it could have been sometime in 1997 or maybe 1998 in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you recall that the Prosecutor asked you several questions yesterday regarding events in Bruska and put to you a report made by security organs, military security organs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the Prosecutor drew your attention in particular to one part of that report, which is a nota bene, in which the author of the report made by the military security service notes that the conclusion that the crime was committed by a sabotage terrorist group is not corroborated by material evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please see on our screens Exhibit 403. That is a document of the 180th Motorised Brigade dated 11th March 1992. My learned friend showed you that document but he did not familiarise you with its contents so I'm going to do that now. You do see the document. That's a report by the 180th Motorised Brigade. Could we please turn to the first working page, with the last digits of the number 6784. Otherwise, in B/C/S it's a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the English translation crosses over onto page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. It looks like my version goes to four pages, and 6784 is the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I omitted to draw your attention to one thing: In the English translation, the first page is marked 3 and continues on page 4. So the first page in English is 3 and the end is on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read the third and the fourth paragraph of this report, the last two paragraphs before the Nota Bene.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it any more, the screen has changed. This is some sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What we see on our screens now is no longer the document we had asked for. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. If I may, I don't think, first of all, that these questions arise out of cross because I used this document for a very narrow purpose of seeing if he was aware of the information in the conclusion. So to go now to read the rest of the document, I don't really -- it doesn't seem to me to arise out of cross. And secondly, this document is in evidence. So we have it. I'm not sure what purpose is served by having the witness read the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor dealt with this case in great detail, and he insisted precisely on the detail that the Defence is now trying to deal with in redirect. My learned friend examined the witness as to whether he had information that the police force was named as a possible perpetrator of this crime in Bruska. He asked him for an answer but he did not show him the contents of the document which proves precisely the opposite. I want to show now that the Prosecutor did not give the witness all information and withheld the information that he had which speaks to the opposite. Of course the Prosecutor is free to choose his material, but he is not allowed, I believe, to misinform the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can you just, for the clarity of the Bench, point us to the information that specifically you want to refer the witness to which the Prosecutor didn't show him and which points to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, paragraphs 3 and 4 of this page. In the English translation, it's page 3. So paragraphs 3 and 4. In other words, the two paragraphs above the Nota Bene. In these two paragraphs, the security officer, who says in the Nota Bene that there is no material evidence to indicate that it was a sabotage terrorist group, does not say that it seems the police perpetrated the crime. On the contrary, he indicates completely different and very specific possible perpetrators, and I think that is important to show to the Trial Chamber and the witness, and the accused, because the accused has the right to counter the theory of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Trial Chamber wants to allow Mr. Milovancevic to proceed on these questions, that's fine, but I do want to make it clear that I certainly in no way misled the witness or withheld information about the witness. I used this document for the specific purpose about the theory of the Croatian Sabotage Unit committing the crime. I didn't address anything about this alternative theory, which is one that the witness in fact touched on. I didn't challenge that. I didn't say there was no evidence to support that. And so there was nothing misleading about the -- my cross-examination. I just wanted that to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, just point quickly to the evidence that you want to point and through the witness. We cannot afford to waste more time on this witness now. We've spent a lot of time on this witness. I'd like to get him out of the Court and I'm sure he wants to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't understand. Do you think it's a waste of time to try to establish facts about one of the most serious charges against Mr. Martic? We have here material that was completely misrepresented by the Prosecutor. He made it out to be exactly the opposite and it will be very brief. The credibility of the witness was attempted at by the Prosecutor by showing him this report concerning Bruska, while the Prosecutor withheld at the same time completely information to the opposite. Which of the two is correct is up to you to decide when you make your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you think I think it's a waste of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's the interpretation of your words that I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard you said, "We are out of time." But I don't know what else we have time for unless we have it for a murder of ten people, a heinous crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want you to read what I said. It's at page 20, line 1. And tell me where it says we are out of time. That's line 1 to line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is written in the first, second, and third line on page 20, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I say "we are out of time"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It says that we cannot waste any more time with this witness or to waste more time on this witness. That's the interpretation I got and it's indeed written in line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You must quote me correctly when you next quote me. And do you -- but did you read that in context? Did you hear what -- did you read what I said first? And are you prepared to do what I asked you to do in that sentence? I would like to get an answer from him before you stand up. Are you prepared to do what I asked you to do in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me to continue, Your Honour. That is what I understood. And I only wanted, as Defence counsel, to point out to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've asked you a question, Mr. Milovancevic. Why don't you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's no answer to my question. Why don't you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I don't understand you, Your Honour. I've lost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. That was the first sentence I said in that statement. Why didn't you do that? That's my question. What is it you don't understand in that question? It's simple and straightforward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are asking me if I'm going to proceed the way you suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if you're going to proceed. I'm asking you why you didn't proceed. Now, again, please listen to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it was very important to me, Your Honour, that this document be shown to the witness, and to the Prosecutor as well, and for the Trial Chamber to hear it in the original, the way it is, because it is completely opposite from what it was held out to be. That's how I wanted to present the material to you, and it is up to you to decide whether you're going to accept my suggestion or not. Now when you told me to ask my question, I'm going to ask the question. This is now situation number 2. I was talking about situation number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... irrelevant to the questions that I'm asking you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm just asking you why you didn't continue when I asked you to continue. It's as simple as all that, and if you don't want to answer me, tell me you don't want to answer me. Before you proceed, Mr. Whiting was on his feet. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I would ask the Trial Chamber to please ask the Defence counsel to refrain from making what I find are baseless suggestions, accusations. The suggestion that I misrepresented this document, I think, is completely groundless and baseless. And I would point out that this document was put into evidence in this trial by the Prosecution. It's something we want the Trial Chamber to be aware of, and I certainly, when asking questions on cross-examination, in no way misrepresented its contents. And Mr. Milovancevic insists on repeating that accusation over and over again. I don't know which crowd he's playing for, but I think it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed inappropriate. And I do not want to go into this any further. Ask your questions, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware that military security organs, when investigating the case in Bruska, also got hold of information available in this document, among others, that a possible motive for the killing of Dusko Marinovic and other members of the Marinovic family was revenge for a brawl wherein the possible perpetrator lost his finger?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After which he was nicknamed Stump.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on re-direct that is a leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, that's a leading question, it does not arise from cross-examination; two reasons for the irrelevance of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I might have misunderstood, but I believe the Trial Chamber had given you permission to proceed to indicate certain passages in the exhibit or the document that is before us to support the questions that -- or the areas that you wished to have dealt with arising properly in the course of cross-examination. So maybe that will help to redirect you. You may have become a little bit distracted by what has happened before, but you're supposed to be indicating the portions, the relevant portions, in the document. That is what you set out to do, and that is what you should be proceeding to now. Will that help you in any way, hopefully?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're more than welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to be able to ask you the following question, I will have to show you a portion of the text. I'm talking about paragraphs 2 and 3, military security. It says: "Through work with an associate named Ranko, a civilian, unvetted, reliable, I learned that about 3 or 4 years ago a serious brawl had erupted between the late Dusko Marinovic and Mile Pupovac, nicknamed Stump, in the brackets, because he lost a finger in the brawl. The brawl occurred in the village of Bruska, and afterwards, Pupovac was taken to the Bijovat [phoen] hospital to get his injuries seen to. Pupovac resides in the village of Medvidja." Next paragraph, paragraph 4 reads: "The associate obtained information to indicate that Mile Pupovac might be one of the perpetrators of this crime and the possible organiser of an act of revenge against Dusko Marinovic. This is in line with the fact that the murders were committed at Dusko Marinovic's house and with the fact that he was one of the first victims. The source then indicates that the others found in Dusko Marinovic's house were killed because they identified the perpetrators and that the only person who remained alive in the house was his daughter-in-law from the village of Dobropoljci." The question in relation to these two paragraphs, Witness, does this text indicate that someone from the police were suspect in this crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text you have just read out does not indicate that the suspects were members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting was on his feet, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's fine. I'll let it go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that in cross examination, the Prosecutor asked you about Arkan's visit to Knin and the fact that he was after that arrested in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that question being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what became of Arkan after the arrest? Was he tried and convicted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read in the press at that time that Arkan was not convicted but was instead soon released from prison in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you done with this document, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I must admit I'm a little bit taken by surprise on the manner in which you dealt with the document just now because I thought what you wanted to get from the witness, if he were aware of these passages which you read to him, or extracts, would he have answered the questions which Mr. Whiting raised to him in cross-examination differently, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all I wanted to do was to use these questions to protect this witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry to have disturbed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember the Prosecutor asking you a number of questions to do with the situation after Operation Maslenica, as well as questions about the attitude of the refugees to the native Croatian population of the area? You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please have on our screen a document from the 65 ter list of the OTP, the number is 345. This is an UNCIVPOL report, Sector South, dated the 8th of February, 1993. Before the document emerges on our monitors, I shall tell you that this is a document in English. There it is. Do you see that in front of you? In the upper right corner it reads "UNCIVPOL Sector South, the 8th of February, 1993, at 1900 hours." Do you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to item 1 of this report entitled "general situation." It reads: "Tensions still high in the area." This is on the 8th of February 1993. It is followed by item 3, further down, it reads: "Operations. UNCIVPOL reports that the Knin civilian police station had submitted a report to the effect that one of their patrols in the village of Vrpolje had come across members of the local police who were guarding the local Croats from that village who had been forced to leave their homes by refugees and who are still residing in schools." At the end of that paragraph we see this: "There were no complaints from the Croats during the visit." In other words, no complaints made to the UNCIVPOL. Does this tally with your knowledge of the situation following Maslenica operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This information tallies with the fact as I know it that the police were guarding those expelled Croats to keep them safe from harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 4; that's 6050 in the English. The second passage, line 2 reads: "A common problem at present is the fact that local Croats are still being expelled from their houses and flats, both by the newly arriving refugees, as well as the local opportunists. Local authorities appear to be powerless to stop this." I will now skip one line in order to save time. And then it follows: "The local authorities said that no persons from now on would be expelled from their homes in this way. They also said that they will have these people returned to their houses and flats. However, these people presently staying in a small school, which is severely overcrowded and has inadequate sanitary facilities, have refused to go back and are adamant that they should be sent to the other side while the Croatian authorities have refused to take them in." Is this a situation that you commented on during your examination-in-chief and cross-examination, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think I commented on this particular situation. I did say a thing or two about a similar situation that occurred in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You heard the Prosecutor ask you about whether it was true that you did not have sufficient manpower because police officers had been deployed along the front line. You did not have enough people to ensure the Croats were safe but you did have enough people to ensure that they left. You remember that question being asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a policy that you and the police force at the time actively pursued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was certainly no official policy that the police pursued or any of the authorities in the area. In Benkovac municipality, there were Croats in great number of villages, in all the areas outside the town of Benkovac itself. In order to make sure that they were safe, an effort like that would have required an enormous number of people, an enormous number of people to provide security for all those villages. We simply didn't have the manpower. It was as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've explained already why it was that you didn't have the manpower required for a task like that, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a war on, and a lot of police officers were sent to the front line to hold the front line in the face of the advancing Croatian forces in the area of Novi Grad and Prigrada [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have several minutes to go before the break and let us now move on to a different subject. Do you remember the Prosecutor showing you Ognjen Biserko's statement? He was an employee of the Secretariat for All People's Defence, the Knin SO, the intelligence centre. This statement has to do with illegal weapons being obtained as well as barricades.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I move on, I move that the document on our screens right now, and I'm talking about the UNCIVPOL report dated the 8th of March, 1993, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it not already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not as far as I know, not as far as my records indicate. This is an OTP exhibit. It's on their 65 ter list, the number is 345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is already Exhibit number 897, according to what the system is telling me. Okay. This will be of course, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Then the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 897.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we now please look at Exhibit 872? This is Mr. Biserko's statement to the then Lieutenant Colonel, Zdravko Tolimir, and recording clerk Zdravko Bicanac [phoen] on the 2nd of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be asked to move closer to the microphone? The interpreters can't hear him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Milovancevic? You are asked to move closer to the microphone because the interpreters can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't catch that, Your Honour. Thanks for warning me. I'm not listening to that channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see this statement? This is Ognjen Biserko's statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will show you the first paragraph in which this witness claims through performing a functional duty at the intelligence centre in Knin, I obtained certain information about illegal semi-military forms of organising and illegal arming of citizens in the Knin territory meant to serve as a defence from an attack by the Special Forces of the Republic of Croatia. I will show you another portion from the next passage. Biserko claims as follows: "I know that a state of war was declared in Knin on the 17th of August, 1990, the purpose being to defend from the special units of the Republic of Croatia which, during the previous night, had tried to seize some of the weapons from the Benkovac and Obrovac public security stations." I'm skipping a sentence, and then the next one, and then I'll wrap it up. "While on duty, I received several different bits of information and misinformation about MUP movement on Obrovac, Benkovac and Knin. I know that after the state of war was declared -- I know that local guards were set up and self-organised in order to defend." About this document, Witness, you spoke about an attempt to secretly seize weapons from the Knin police station. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that this attempt ensued after an attempted intervention by Croatia's special police units?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's a leading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Please sit down. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection, it's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You hear that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Indeed I do. I withdraw the question. I think this is a convenient time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take the break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, a while ago we looked at a portion of Ognjen Biserko's statement. My question is: Which day was it that pursuant to an order of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia that you tried to seize weapons from the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two different times. The first was between the 16th and the 17th of August, and the second was on the 17th of August at about 1200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did the break-in into the weapons depot of the reserve police forces in Knin occur? Was that before or after your attempts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seizure of weapons occurred afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Thank you. Do you remember being asked by the Prosecutor in cross-examination whether the speeches made by the Serb leaders in Krajina saying that the government was an Ustasha government were making people scared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at Exhibit 237? Before the document appears on our screens, Witness, this is a transcript of a conversation dated the 14th of October, 1990, between Ministers Martin Spegelj and Josip Boljkovac. Can you please tell us what sort of minister Martin Spegelj was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Croatia's Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for Josip Boljkovac, you said he was the minister who appointed you and because of whom you were called an Ustasha. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a document in English on the screen in front of you? This is a conversation of the 14th of October, 1990. I will read the first paragraph out to you. Martin Spegelj says: "Listen, if the need arises at a crucial moment, find two or three men to get rid of the most dangerous ones."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOLJKOVAC REPLIES
utterances.text: "All right." Martin Spegelj goes on to say: "Get them to get rid of them physically. Somebody goes to the flat, a courier. He appears at the door. Bang, bang, bang. Then goes down the stairs." Josip Boljkovac replies: "And then they call the police to ask who had done that." Martin Spegelj proceeds: "Then he goes down the stairs, goes to the next one, kills the next one, too, at the same time and that's that. The most dangerous ones must be killed at their doorstep, regardless of the women and children, regardless of anything." Witness, do you understand this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have here Croatia's defence minister asking the minister the interior to make some people available for some killings. Does that not appear to be a fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure how this arises out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor tried to use his questions to elicit from the present witness an answer to the following question: Were the people in Krajina scared because their own politicians had scared them for no reason at all? I am now showing an OTP document indicating that this was done because the government was referred to as an Ustasha government. Now I'm showing an OTP document with two crucial ministers in Croatia's government negotiating on how they would have some people killed, and I'm merely asking the witness whether that is his understanding as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does that got to do by scaring Serbs by calling Croatians Ustashas? In this document you had it when you led this witness. You could have led on it when you did lead the witness. I'm not sure why -- I don't see the relationship to what you put to the witness, that the Serb leaders called Croatian government Ustashas. We know that people were being killed on both sides. That's a fact. But what has that got to do with the term "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point in time, we know nothing. We are trying to ascertain the facts. The Prosecutor claims that the people in Krajina had no reason to fear the Croatian government. He speaks about the moral credibility of the government being referred to as an Ustasha government and claims that that gave the people reason to fear. I am proceeding with this document. This is a very important document, and I'm moving on to something else in the document which I'm showing the witness in a minute. As I proceed, you will see the reasoning behind this line of questions. So please, Your Honour, allow me to proceed. An objection was raised as to why I hadn't done it previously. The reason was I got from the witness answers which I had been expecting and which I was happy with. Now the Prosecutor is trying to represent those same answers in a different light. I'm using this OTP document to show that it's not what the Prosecutor claims it to be but something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Milovancevic, you don't just ask questions that you want to get. You ask questions also that advance your case. And if you were aware of this document and you wanted to show that two ministers in the Croatian government negotiated what you say they negotiated, you could have done so. In any case, this document is an exhibit. You say you call it Exhibit 237. The Chamber is going to read it. It's going to see that, but it does not answer the allegation that Serb leaders called Croatian government an Ustasha government with the view to putting fear in the Serb people. It just does not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, I think it is exactly the opposite of what you say, with due respect, because this document is a document of the Prosecution. It was disclosed to us three years ago and it has been exhibited. Despite the fact that it has been exhibited, in this document, Minister Boljkovac says, "We will use all means," and you will see that in the text below. And, "We will resolve the problem of Knin with weapons. Knin shall perish." And the other minister says, "The problem will be resolved by massacre." And although this has been exhibited and it's on the record, my learned friend insists on a completely different theory saying that there was no fear, and the only fear was one artificially created with false stories about people being in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it's necessary, but I think that the Defence is misstating the position of the Prosecution. The Prosecution is -- the position of the Prosecution is that the fears were exaggerated by the Serb leaders, in part by using the term "Ustasha" and making references to World War II. So I don't think -- I don't think that this arises, and it's also information -- this is something I believe it's on the record that this isn't something that came out until January of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm trying to get you to understand one thing here. The purpose of re-examination is to clear points that had remained unclear during cross-examination. The point you are now pursuing did not arise on cross-examination, and you are now eliciting completely new evidence which justifies a cross-examination. Now, I -- if you'll let me finish. Now, I understand the Defence case, what the Defence case is. This is what you are now doing is what you should have done when you were leading your witness. And I'm saying to you this document is in evidence. The Chamber is going to see this document, and what you are pointing out to the witness right now the Chamber is going to see. If you want to show this witness this document, I have no problems with that, but you must then answer the allegation by the Prosecution. The allegation by the Prosecution is that the Serb leaders called the government of Croatia Ustashas in order to instill fear amongst the Serbs. You've got to show me how this document answers that or clarifies that. It doesn't seem to clarify that. And I'm afraid much as it -- you may want to proceed with it, I don't see how you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend just gave an explanation why I am asking these questions in redirect. My learned friend says that these stories about Ustasha government were an exaggeration of fear. Despite all the witness has said about his own fears and the fears of others during examination-in-chief, and that was corroborated by material, my learned friend insists that the fear was exaggerated, and that is why I want you, Your Honours, to hear the witness speak about the materials I'm going to show him to rebut the theory of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is not the time to rebut, Mr. Milovancevic. This is the time to clarify. The time to rebut was when you led your witness. This is what I'm trying to say to you. This time you can't be leading new evidence. And I'm afraid I must rule you out of order, Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry, you can't ask any further questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I just want to say one more thing. I'm not presenting new documents. This is a document already in evidence that the Prosecutor is completely ignoring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't say you're presenting a new document. I said new evidence. This point is in evidence. I've been saying that to you. I know it is in evidence. The Chamber is going to be read it. It's going to be aware of what these two ministers said to each other, and it's going to read all the other documents that both you and the Prosecution have put into evidence but did not read entirely. You pointed us to certain parts of it, but we are going to read the entire documents and we will take the entire document into consideration. That is why the document goes into evidence. You don't have to repeat -- you don't have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but then with such an approach of the Trial Chamber, redirect is pointless. I'm not happy with one answer of the witness alone. I am trying to see what he actually meant, and I'm asking him additional questions that should provide me with the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on this point. Okay? Can you proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to questions by the Prosecutor, you spoke about the Croatian government and said that it had legal grounds to seize weapons from the reserve police force. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in response to questions from the Prosecution you explained that a buildup of the reserve police force was much higher than actually needed and that only Croats were admitted and that Croat ethnicity was the key criterion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that you explained that Ante Bujas, in agreement with the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, explained to you that weapons were seized from the reserve police force in order to arm those new Croatian policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but those last two things were things that were not on cross-examination, were on direct examination, the fact that only Croats were admitted and the Croat ethnicity was a key criterion. Unless I've forgotten, I don't believe I asked any questions about that, and I asked only about the size of the police force. And the next question is also, I don't believe, something I touched on in cross-examination. I think that was elicited on direct examination,. Unless I'm mistaken and can be pointed to the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to point us to the page, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the objection of the Prosecution. That will not change the purpose of my further questions. I accept the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for accepting the objection. And then can I tell you my complaint with those three questions is that you're just asking him if he remembers things and he says yes. Now, I would like you to ask him questions so that he gives you the answer, not that you give him the answer and then he confirms the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I have just reached that point. I wanted to ask two or three background questions before the last one that I'm going to ask of him now. I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the establishment of a mono-ethnic police force in a multi-ethnic state represent a legal act?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that the Prosecutor showed you an interview of Mr. Martic from August 1990, in which he says that he belongs to the people's police, that he is against the Croatian government that is creating evil and that he will only obey the people? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this testimony, both in direct examination and in cross-examination, there was a lot of talk about fear from genocide, either genuine or created by artificial means. Were your fears justified by actual events eventually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The things that were talked about at the time and that were feared came true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I don't like to interfere with your cross-examination [sic]. You have asked a question which I thought was laying a foundation. Do you recall that the Prosecutor showed you an interview by Mr. Martic? Now the question doesn't follow from that interview. You're now asking him about his fears. Now, those fears you should have led him about them in examination-in-chief. What arises out of this interview? Go to the interview. That's why you put that as a foundation. Please stay relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate your suggestion as entirely to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will withdraw my last question, Witness. Let me ask you another one. The convictions of Mr. Martic expressed in his public speeches to the effect that he was fighting the Croatian government that was creating evil, did it prove correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His approach proved to be a correct one, especially because it turned out that the Croatian side did not have much desire to hold talks and to find a solution. The situation as it developed heralded a war with large casualties on the Serbian side from 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, may I start with the last point? This interview where we saw a video clip, the interview of Milan Martic in August 1990, did you see that at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it on Croatian TV when it was broadcast back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber, Mr. Witness, would like to continue asking you a few questions, and this is the question that I would like you to answer, one of the questions, starting with this one: When serious crimes had been committed, such as the murder of several people in the village, in a particular village, would you normally report such information immediately to the Knin Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, whenever a report came in or something like that occurring, we would regularly go to the crime scene, we would carry out an investigation, gather all the possible indicia, and any information that was found on the scene in order to help us track down the perpetrator. We would immediately send a dispatch to a body that was our direct superior. In this case, it was the Knin SUP. If the number of casualties was higher, such as two or three people killed, we would immediately inform the Ministry of the Interior in Knin. Whenever we inspected crime scenes in accordance with the law on criminal procedure, which represented rules that applies to us, we would normally inform the Court as well with an investigating magistrate present as well as a prosecutor. Whenever crimes were more serious. We couldn't just gloss over them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm pleased to hear that. But could you tell us further who you -- you or your superiors would report to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would submit a report to the district and public prosecutors. Crimes that can be punished by sentence of up to five years are reported to the district Prosecutor. Serious crimes are reported to the public prosecutor who was in this case based in Knin. And then work continues and other steps are taken. Any later results are submitted in a special report to the prosecutor, informing the prosecutor of all our actions and results. This only stopped once a case was resolved, or else a case could remain open until further notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In terms of the Knin Ministry of the Interior, which particular person or officer in the Ministry of the Interior would you report to in sending in these reports that you mentioned when it was more serious, that you sent in the reports? Could you give an indication to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior in Knin, as well as smaller, lower-level units, had a duty service, and they were receiving all the information from all over Krajina, all incoming reports. We would normally send a dispatch to whichever department was on duty at the time. In the Ministry of the Interior there was a duty officer who on the day of his duty was responsible for the work of the entire ministry, in the absence of the minister, his deputy and all the other high-ranking officials. He was immediately notified about everything and aware of everything that was going on. Whenever he had anything to add or to request, he would make phone calls to us or send us a dispatch with his requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And would he in turn report to the deputy and the minister, that officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have been duty-bound to submit reports on such events to the Ministry of the Interior. Normally that report was submitted to the minister, his deputy and a number of heads of sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to go on to another area. You stated that Mr. Martic, as president of the RSK, once ordered that all perpetrators of serious crimes be arrested, particularly murderers, and that these perpetrators were tried for a variety of reasons -- sorry, that these perpetrators were tried but for a variety of reasons they were not detained in prison and that they were eventually released. Now, do you recall when this order was issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that was in 1994, but I can't remember the specific date when this order was issued. I remember that I was out on a mission in Benkovac at the time. We acted upon that order and we brought some persons into the Knin station, from where they were taken to Stara Gradiska, the reason being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, that's what I was going to ask you. What crimes were they under suspicion for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under suspicion for murder and murder alone, not any misdemeanors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What ethnic group did the persons under suspicion belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And the victims, what ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were members of both ethnic groups among the victims, both Serb and Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In this instant case that you're speaking about, the victims were both Serb and Croat, you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. There were both Croats and Serbs among the victims and the perpetrators were, for God knows what reason, released and awaited trial. For some reason, I think they couldn't secure sufficient witnesses because of the war and the ongoing clashes. Eventually an order was given for all of them to be arrested and taken to prison for a new trial or in order to expedite the existing proceedings. The idea was to isolate those perpetrators, not just leave them at large, but instead lock them away in order to protect everybody else from them. I can only say that I met this decision with great enthusiasm, although the decision itself was probably not based on any existing law at the time but more a result of the circumstances that prevailed amid a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: These tell me, those perpetrators, did they belong to a particular unit; and if they did, please tell us which unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrators were for the most part military. They were members of the army. I think I can say that with certainty, simply because most of the Krajina army were professional soldiers who had been trained to become soldiers. If you look at certain types of information, such as Interpol arrest warrants, you will see that not so frequent among those are professionals or police officers. The majority is constituted by civilians who became soldiers and then committed certain crimes. But the UNCIVPOL knew about this. There is no doubt about that. Because during our talks, they would certainly not have allowed for potential perpetrators to continue to work as police officers. Certainly most of the police force comprised professionals who were well trained to do their job and not people like these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. But you have said that they were part of the military. Could you give an indication, you cast your mind back, be more specific, which particular unit or corps? Would you be able to say at this stage? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order given by Mr. Martic at the time was in reference to the entire Krajina area. I remember the specific case at Benkovac. I had several such cases, in fact, and we took in such persons and took them to our superior command as had been indicated in our instructions. They were then taken to Stara Gradiska near Okucani, which was located in Sector West under the then UNPROFOR geographical division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the judicial bodies for all sorts of reasons, both objective and subjective, neglected their duties and failed to carry out their tasks and that because of that, Mr. Martic had to issue an order. That is Milan Martic. Do you know what legal basis there was for Mr. Martic to issue such an order to detain people? Are you able to say? Please tell us what the basis was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the citizens and soldiers along the front line in the town and elsewhere had a huge grievance against those persons who had been suspected of murder. There was a public outcry because these people were still walking around freely. This had an adverse effect on general morale. And that was probably the reason that Martic made this decision. I'm not sure which law he based this decision on at the time, but it was probably based on some authority he enjoyed, simply because a state of war had been declared. Be that as it may, it wasn't my job to question the justification behind that order because it was an order that I had received from my direct superior. All I had to do was to have it implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So in fact there might not have been any authority in law for him to carry out this act by virtue of his office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility, but it's not for me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could you also let me know whether you were talking about one or two orders issued by Mr. Martic, and also tell us exactly what you were ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about a single order issued by him, an order that we received in a dispatch that was telexed to us from Knin. It said that the substance applied to the entire territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. We were ordered to arrest those people, take them to the Knin command, and it was specified that they would later be sent to Sector West. Certain measures were taken. No weapons were used during that particular arrest, and these people were arrested such as people are arrested in any other country. Their hands were tied to keep them from trying to escape. That sort of measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Do you know whether these persons were ever brought before a court or a judge to determine the legality of their detention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was a committee set up by the justice ministry reviewing earlier cases in which persons were brought in. It was based on this that they expedited a number of their proceedings and they started getting some work done. I believe this led at the time to a number of convictions. That's as far as my recollection of that specific case goes, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And were these persons civilians, or were they not?
