utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among those persons detained at the time, there were both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Which unit would the soldiers have come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers came from a variety of units. The group comprised 20 to 30 persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And which were those variety of units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, or rather specifically I remember something that happened in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I'm going to try and be brief with you Mr. -- I'm sorry, I can't call your name. Sometime today you were asked by the Prosecutor -- or, rather, I think it was put to you by the Prosecutor that Davor Lukic was detained at the Benkovac public security police station, and you said, no, he was in the barracks and later ended up with the misdemeanours magistrate. Do you remember that testimony by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did you come to know that he was in the barracks and later ended up with a misdemeanours magistrate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may expand a little on this. In this case I was involved too. This was back in 2000, when I received word that there was an Interpol arrest warrant out against me, that I was suspected of mistreatment and inflicting grievous bodily harm against a person named Davor Lukic. I thought hard about it, and I just couldn't seem to remember when this happened or where, or who that person was. There were four other persons in addition to myself who were accused of these actions at the time, and I started looking into the matter. I managed to find out about the remaining four persons, who they were. I knew two of them, and two were unfamiliar. I knew two of these persons from before, because they used to work in Benkovac at the police station. I tracked down their addresses and these persons at the time were residing in Serbia. On one of my trips to Serbia, I went to their homes. We talked, and after a while I asked them about this incident and they told me as follows. Davor Lukic is a person they used to know from before because he resided in their village, the same village as those two police officers, or perhaps an adjacent village, but they all knew each other. That was the gist. That day, the evening or night of that day, a civilian came from the Republic of Croatia and approached the place where those two police officers were standing. This was during a cease-fire, when there was no fighting. These two police officers were members of the border police at the Stabanj border crossing, a border crossing along the Benkovac-Biograd road. This civilian approached them peacefully and when they laid eyes on him they knew immediately that he was a Croat and that he was on his way from Croatia. They IDed him and searched him. They found a pistol on him and they claimed that the pistol was loaded. They took him to a local station, police station, along the border. It used to be a cafe, a catering establishment before the war but was now converted to be used as a provisional police station. They searched him and after that, they called in the military. They called the nearby barracks. A military vehicle arrived and this person was taken to Benkovac. After an interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must interrupt you, Mr. Witness. You've told me a whole page, you have still not answered my question. I just want to know one simple little thing: When did you come to know of the fact that Davor Lukic was held in the barracks and later transferred to the misdemeanours magistrate? I've been waiting very patiently for this answer. It's not coming. That's why I'm interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to come to this detail that he was taken into custody, into the barracks, in 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please answer my question. Thank you for all that speech. Now answer my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 2000, 2001, approximately, when I found those two young men, policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you when you found policemen. I'm asking when you came to know that Davor Lukic was kept in the barracks and later ended up with misdemeanours magistrate. You see, it is these long answers that you give that make you forget what the question is. I'm not asking you about two young men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out in 2000 or in 2001, when I found those two young men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You also testified about cooperation that you established between yourselves as the police in Serbian Krajina with UNCIVPOL. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What exactly did the orders to cooperate entail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand, Your Honour. What do you mean "orders to cooperate"? What is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your testimony at transcript 6882 to 883 says: "We had orders to establish cooperation with them, and I don't think it is my personal achievement in that area. It is a result of what we were asked to do, what we were instructed to do, the entire police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had the same instructions, to cooperate with the UN force." What did the order entail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I understand. It was a telegram, a dispatch that I received from my superiors, Secretariat of the Interior of Knin, which was my superior station, invoking another dispatch that arrived from the Ministry of the Interior. So that is the procedure whether another -- when a dispatch from a superior instance arrives, a similar dispatch is made downward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I stop you? What did the order entail? Just tell me the contents of the order. I don't want to know the procedure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall now, it said roughly that we should extend all possible assistance to the United Nations civilian police in their movement, to provide them with security by forming joint patrols, and to provide them with information about whichever case they may be interested in, and to try to establish a system of work wherein, if we find that they are giving us useful advice, we should act according to that advice, and that's what we did, upon which we compiled reports about our cooperation with the United Nations CIVPOL and submitted these reports to our superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who issued the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time the Ministry of the Interior was Mr. Martic. I think he signed it. Because the dispatch from Knin said that it was a dispatch coming from the ministry, higher up, so it was probably the minister or his deputy who wrote the original order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you receive the order in writing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such orders are sent in the form of a telegram, a dispatch, in writing. A telegram would arrive from your superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would a telegram show a signature of the author?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no telegram on which you can see a signature because that is the technique of transmission. It's not like a fax or a scan. It's a different system, typing a wire, using the Morse code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you this question, because you were suggesting that it was signed by Mr. Martic. My question really is: How do you know it was signed by Mr. Martic if it was a telegram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the dispatch that I received from Knin, they were invoking a corresponding dispatch from the Ministry of the Interior because the Secretariat in Knin was the link between my station in Benkovac and the Ministry of Croatia. Let me give you an example. Usually a dispatch usually begins with the words, "Pursuant to a dispatch from the MUP of the RSK, we hereby" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the corresponding dispatch contain an order to cooperate with UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that dispatch, we were told to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the content of the corresponding dispatch, the prior dispatch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, in that prior dispatch, just a summary was given, whereas the lower command provided more detail when conveying that summary to the lower ranking unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the corresponding dispatch, in what form did it come? Did it come by way of a telegram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch from the ministry to the Knin SUP probably arrived by means of cable, in the form of a telegram, but it could also have arrived in the letter -- in the form of a letter, with a signature, because both of these institutions were in Knin. And sometimes such documents were delivered by courier because the buildings of the two institutions were close by, in the same town, in Knin. Both the Knin SUP and the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Krajina were in Knin. If we are talking about the technical aspect of delivery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You actually don't know how the corresponding dispatch came, and in what form?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I'm just assuming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you cannot even say whether it was signed itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know whether it was signed. I'm just saying that it was only the minister or his deputy who could have issued it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, you cannot say the latter dispatch was signed by the minister basing that on the assumption that it relates to the previous dispatch, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. The dispatch sent to me was never signed by the minister. It was signed by my immediate superior, the secretary of the SUP. It was not only that one. Never would a minister sign the dispatch sent to lower-ranking units. He only signed the original order, the original dispatch. The follow-up dispatches would be signed by chiefs of lower-ranking units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand you now. I thought earlier you had said, which is why we were talking about Mr. Martic, you said he had signed it now, and then you changed and said no, it cannot be signed because it's a telegram. Now it is suddenly signed by your immediate superior, the secretary of the SUP. Which is which between these three versions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, without going into the contents of the dispatch, let me say this briefly. The MUP sends a dispatch to Knin regarding lower-ranking units. The SUP of Knin then takes this dispatch received either in writing or as a telegram, forwards this dispatch to lower units. In their dispatch, they invoke the prior dispatch and fleshes out the orders given to the lower-ranking unit, and that second dispatch is signed by the secretary, by the secretary of the Secretariat of the SUP. This second dispatch does not contain the first one. It only invokes the first one. It says "with reference to."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we will get to the bottom of this question. Let's move on to the next one. Now, before this instruction to cooperate, was there any contact between the Ministry of the Interior in Knin and UNCIVPOL on which information would be provided by the police stations to UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there existed contacts on that level between the ministry and the chief of sector. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Later, you're telling me about something that happened later. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this sentence, I, and then the witness named his position, could be identifying for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Page 58, line starting at line 10 -- sentence starting at line 10 to 13, may it please be redacted? I interrupted you, sir, because you were telling me about something that took place later, whereas my question was asking you about something that took place before. My question to you was: Before you received these orders to cooperate, had there been any contact between the Ministry of the Interior of Knin and the UNCIVPOL on which information would be provided to the police, by the police stations to UNCIVPOL? You said yes, there had been. I was going to ask you the nature of that contact, but then you moved on to telling me what happened after. Are you able to tell me the nature of the contact that existed before you received this order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my first contacts with the CIVPOL were when the officers of Norwegian police arrived; in fact, the officer. He was scouting to find a good base for his police station. That was just in April 1992, just after I arrived in that town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when did you receive the order to cooperate with these UN forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, that notification arrived just after we had our first contacts. It was in fact an instruction on how we must behave towards representatives of the UNCIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know if other police stations provided information directly to UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was compulsory for everybody in Sector South, because I attended those meetings. Dalmatia and Lika was required to assist based on the agreements reached between us. I don't know about the other sectors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did you receive any guidance from the Ministry of the Interior as to which information was to be provided to the UN forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not get any guidance from the ministry. For the most part, we agreed that at meetings attended by secretaries of Knin and Korenica SUPs, and also by all the rest of us, subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we -- I've lost track.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we are five minutes beyond the break time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry. Maybe I should turn over to somebody when I'm asking questions. May we take the break and come back at quarter to 6.00. I'm awfully sorry. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Do you know whether Mr. Milan Martic had any contact with UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that he had any contacts with UNCIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How would you then describe Mr. Milan Martic's involvement in investigations into crime in the period 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for his investigations into that, I don't know that he conducted any. The investigations were conducted by inspectors on the ground, together with their superiors. I don't see why he as a minister should conduct investigations. He was probably kept informed. In fact, he was kept informed about the course of the investigations through reports. But that he conducted any himself, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But would you say in any case that he was aware of what was going on in the police stations? I hear you say he was to be kept informed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking based on my experience. I did report to my immediate superior command, and I believe others did as well. So based on such reports, he was supposed to be informed of what was going on. It is, of course, possible that somebody failed to inform him. I don't know, and I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You spoke through your testimony about special police units. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also indicated that these police units were involved in military work and border duties. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the special units that I referred to were used in police operations, but they were also involved in military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And border guarding too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, special police units were not deployed on the border because there was not enough personnel, and it was not necessary anyway. It was the military who secured the borders and, before that, the units that were called special units of the police that were later militarised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "at that time," which time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the time between the first part of the war until the UNPROFOR arrived and was deployed in June 1992, until the beginning of Maslenica 3 aggression. Those were special units of the police at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do not have the reference with me, but I specifically remember you saying -- mentioning border duty as one of their jobs, one of their duties. Are you saying that was not part of their job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember stating that special police guarded the border. They manned just border crossings. At border crossings, there were deployed police units that belonged to secretariats of internal affairs, of which there were seven in RSK. Their job was to control border crossings, and UNCIVPOL called these border crossings check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the difference between border crossings and borders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, border crossings were roads connecting the Republic of Serbian Krajina with Bosnia and Herzegovina and Vojvodina in Serbia, and also the RSK with Croatia. Those were thoroughfares on which there was traffic of people, vehicles, et cetera, whereas the border is the line delimiting the entire Krajina. At that time, it was guarded by specialised units of the police. That's what they were called. And at border crossings there were simple police units who were based in SUPs, secretariats of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I would like to -- I would like to understand you very clearly, because now you're talking of borders guarded by specialised units of the police, and I'm asking you about the duties of the special police units. Is there a difference between specialised units of the police and special police units? Are these two different entities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may have been a misinterpretation. What I would like to do is show you or draw for you what a border crossing meant. Border crossings were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? I understood what you meant by border crossings. I understand that by border crossings you're talking of check-points on the roads within the SAO Krajina. And borders you're talking about the borders of the country outside. I understand that. I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking about specialised units of the police and special police units. Are these two different entities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are two different bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you said -- this is where I get the question of borders from, and please correct it if I'm wrong, there were two different kinds of formation. Units that were in charge of policing, police work, and special purpose units whose task was to watch the borders, to a lower extent, and also to cooperate with the civilian element of UNPROFOR. That's your evidence yesterday. And then the correction said, no, with the military element of UNPROFOR. Do you remember that evidence? And I'm not pinning you down to saying that their job should be the borders. I'm just saying that's what you said yesterday. And I understand your clarification that by borders then yesterday you meant border crossings. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, specialised police units worked with the military component of UNPROFOR, whereas the civilian police were the public security stations. And only that small amount who worked at border crossings and let people through actually worked with UNCIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean by "only that small amount"? Small amount of what and what is small amount, in terms of quantity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say a small amount, all I mean is the road being controlled by members of the police who were few, and these people belonged to the SUPs, to the secretariats of internal affairs. As for areas between two border crossings, these distances were sometimes as huge as 30 kilometres, and those were guarded by specialised police units. The distances in between. And they were the ones working with the military component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now don't confuse me. These specialised police units were called special police units, were they not? And they controlled border crossings? Are we agreed on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not the ones controlling the border crossings. They were just guarding the border from incursions by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The external border of the country, the boundaries of the entire country; that is, the boundaries of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The boundaries of Croatia or the boundaries of Yugoslavia or the boundaries of SAO Krajina? Which boundaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The boundaries of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, who worked on the border crossings inside SAO Krajina? The civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian police worked at border crossings which were also along SAO Krajina's borders. There were no internal borders within SAO Krajina. But it was members of UNCIVPOL that refused to call these border crossings because the Croats complained. Rather, they elected to refer to them as check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. That's -- don't confuse us. You see, when you start giving long answers -- I'm trying to get clarity here. And I put my questions in such a way that if you answer me yes or no, you'll have given me the full answer I want. Your explanations confuse me further. Now I ask you again: The civilian police are the ones who worked on the border crossings, what CIVPOL called check-points?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these civilian police wore uniforms when they worked there, or didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And I would like to get clarity. There is an allegation -- maybe let me back-track a little bit. Were they ever accompanied by other people who were not in uniform, civilian people, for instance, on their duties on the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could not control those border crossings with no uniform. This is traffic control and it's done wearing a uniform. There are prescriptions to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what did they do on the border crossings? What were they doing? I would imagine that traffic is normally controlled by the traffic signs. Why was -- why were they on border crossings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the end of June 1992 and the 22nd of January, 1993, between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Croatia, there had been a wave of migrations, and also UNPROFOR forces began to move. CIVPOL were transporting people who needed to travel from one area to the other. Sometimes there was a death in a family and people needed to travel, and that's why traffic occurred along these roads. Things were being said to the effect that the population would begin to shift from Krajina into Croatia and back, and we set up these stations in order to control these waves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you were working in Knin all the time, I'm talking about the entire period that you were there, did you ever come to hear of the term "Martic's Police"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did it mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across the term in Croatian media. My understanding at the time was they used the term to mean the entire police force in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or even something much broader, sometimes even all the citizens who were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You also testified, and I think this was yesterday, that the specialised police who had -- who were police already, received further training at Golubic. Am I correct? Am I interpreting your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The already-existing police stations and units in 1991, some of them volunteered to go to receive further training at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you ever go there for further training yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what further training was provided at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Golubic camp was set up after the operation at Plitvice and the clashes with the Croatian side, the Croatian police. That's when the need arose to set up specialised units of the police that were meant to protect the people and SAO Krajina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question: Do you know what further training they received at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't undergo training at Golubic myself, nor was I ever there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You answered that question already. My question is simply: Do you know what further training was provided to these police at Golubic? If you don't know, it's no sin. Just say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't know things that you were at only. You know things that you haven't seen. You have not been to the sun but you do know there is a sun, don't you? And have you been to the sun? Then answer my question. That's why I say you must listen to the question and answer it correctly. I'm saying: Do you know what further training was provided at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was additional physical and military training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what you think. I'm asking you what you know. Do you know or don't you know? Please listen to the question and answer the question. And I say, if you don't know, nobody is going to harass you for that. I just want to know if you know or you don't know. But please answer questions relevantly. Do you know or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I wasn't there, but I heard about it. And I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want me to let the record show that you're refusing to answer this question or is there any reason you can't answer me? I don't think my question is such a complicated question. I'm not asking you whether you were there. I'm just asking if you do know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do. What was the further training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you. I have no further questions. Mr. Milovancevic, any questions arising from the questions by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. None. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Very few, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I just have three or four questions. You testified in response to Her Honour Judge Nosworthy's questions that in respect to the -- those arrests that were made in 1994 that the perpetrators were for the most part military. Do you recall that answer that you gave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then you were asked some questions about what units they belonged to, and I just want to clarify one thing. When you say they are military, I take it you mean they were members of the RSK army, the Republika Srpska Krajina army? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the RSK army, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, to the extent that you know, were the crimes, the murders for which these individuals were arrested, were they committed while the individuals were in the RSK army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a question about the army. Was this particular person on duty or off duty at the time? I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I guess there are two parts to the question. First, were they even in the army at all at the time that the alleged murder was committed; and then secondly, do you know whether at the time the alleged murder was committed they were on duty or off duty? Do you know that information or is that information that you do not know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, please allow me to explain there. Along the line where there was an army presence, there was no population and no villages as a result of the long-raging war. Murders could only have been committed further off from the front line in the hinterland but then they would have been off duty, wouldn't they? Most of the crimes were not committed while these soldiers were on duty somewhere along the front line but, rather, when they why free, when they were off. They could still have been members of the army but they had a day off, and they would be back on duty the next day. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Now, my next question is: At the time they were arrested in 1994, were they still members of the RSK army? At the time they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, most of them still were, but maybe some weren't. Because, after all, the area in question is quite large, and I wasn't receiving reports from all over Krajina submitted to me for analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm only asking to the extent you know, not about things you don't know. So with regard to the cases that you knew about or that you were involved with, in those cases, were the individuals that were arrested still members of the RSK army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I understand from that answer that some were. Some were; some were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some were, that's true. Quite right when you say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, finally, you were just asked about the term "Martic's Police," and you said that you heard about it in the Croatian media. Isn't it a fact that this was a term that was also used by Serbs in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some Serbs used that term, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And isn't it the case also that some members of the police in the SAO Krajina used that term, referred to themselves as Martic's Police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that particular piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness. This brings us to the end of your testimony. The Chamber takes this opportunity to thank you for coming to testify. We understand that you should be a busy person and you take time off from your busy schedule. It's much appreciated. Once again, thank you for coming and you are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours. I also wish to thank you everybody in this courtroom, all the parties. I sincerely hope that I have contributed to the success of this trial to some extent at least. I wish you every luck in your future work as well as a successful conclusion to this trial. I also wish you every luck in your private lives. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you calling your witness, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are ready to call the next witness. We have about 20 minutes left and I think we should be off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's as long as the Chamber agrees. Perhaps the Chamber believes that it's better to start the witness anew on Monday. We would certainly not be opposing that proposal. We don't have much time left in today's session, after all. We can elicit personal information from the witness, but we can't do more than mere technicalities with the remaining time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just that the Chamber has some housekeeping to handle and we could use this time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have one thing to share with the Chamber. The witness's visa expires on Wednesday which leaves us with Monday and Tuesday to deal with the witness, both in chief and in cross. I sincerely believe this is something that we can accomplish. But that's what I wanted to share with you. I think it's important and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will understand, Mr. Milovancevic, that you are in control of that. If you ask short questions and you elicit short answers, we might be able to achieve that. But my question to you is: Do you want to call him? If you want to call him, you can call him. The Chamber has some housekeeping to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That should be fine. I think we can go straight to our housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the Chamber is very seriously concerned about time. This witness, according to the Defence estimate, should have been here for seven hours. By the time Mr. Milovancevic, you were through, with your evidence-in-chief, he had gone well beyond ten hours. Now, I'm trying to be conservative because I just don't have a clear memory on what time he started on the day he started to testify, but certainly he had gone beyond ten hours. It could have been 12. Now, I'm sure you are aware of the Rule 73 ter notice decision that was handed down, which has cut down the Defence time by some 40 hours, and we've got to try and fit in, okay, in the time scheduled. We are not likely to do so at the rate at which we are going, if we are going to go according to the time we took on this witness. I'm saying this and I'm trying to be very cool about it. I'm saying to you, we realise -- you indicated yesterday that you're cutting down your witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move into private session very quickly? May we move into private session, please?.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, before you proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, your learned friend was on his feet. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It was simply that, that exact point about open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We will later enumerate the various positions you held in that public security station and in SUP Sibenik. Can you tell us whether those good interpersonal and intra-ethnic relations in Drnis continued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relations were as I qualified them until January 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened then? Did anything change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. When the multi-party elections were announced, relations were disrupted in the whole town, in the municipality, but also in the station itself, to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say the relations among ethnicities and among people were disrupted, you mentioned multi-party elections. When were they held? Which elections do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely when the law prescribed or scheduled those elections, but already in August 1990 the pre-election campaign started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you described the atmosphere in the town of Drnis and in your own workplace, you said relations among people were very good, even excellent, and you said there was a change after the elections were scheduled. How was that change felt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the station itself, the change manifested itself because one policeman was dismissed for failing to perform his duties, and then he was returned to his job under the pressure of powerful people from the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that mean that his return somehow disrupted relations within the station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His return did not disrupt the relations but it marked the beginning of distrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened outside of the police station, in the town and in the municipalities, in view of those elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town and in the municipality, rallies began to be held. At first, it was only smaller groups of people who were involved, but as time passed, it began to look like a major happening. Larger and larger crowds gathered to attend those rallies. The gathering of large crowds inclined to certain behaviour was subject to sanctions in the republic and federal law, and there began to be expressed a Serbophobia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of gatherings do you mean? Cultural? Sports events? What kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant rallies for the Croatian Democratic Union which used prohibited iconography, wherein representatives of the HDZ behaved like SS detachments in the Second World War. They chanted certain songs, used certain forms of salute, including a particular Ustasha salute from the Second World War. There were popular celebrations with oxen roasted on the spit, the use of flags which were then prohibited, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Talking about all these flags that were being flown, which were the ones that were allowed and which were the ones that were not allowed at the time? You're talking about early 1990, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only flags allowed at the time was the SFRY flag with a five-pointed star and the flag of the Republic of Croatia which also had a star.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say "the Republic of Croatia," what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Socialist Republic of Croatia. When I say the SFRY, that stands for the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say those were HDZ rallies, political rallies. Can I ask you directly, were these pre-election rallies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were these HDZ rallies only at the municipal level or were there other rallies that were organised at other levels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These rallies weren't just at the municipal level, at least at the time, and I can't give you the exact month. Franjo Tudjman himself attended one of these. There were also other representatives of the HDZ from Split and other major Croatian towns in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mentioned some songs that people were chanting at those rallies and some battle cries, if I may call them that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you several examples that might require some interpreting. The first to come were the salutes, ready for the homeland, accompanied by a fascist salute with an arm raised. The next one was a song that went this way: My little knife, spattered with blood, all you want is Serbian flesh, Serbian liver. And the next one said: It's not wine that we Croats drink. What we drink is the blood of Serbs from Knin. And all the Ustasha things and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you used the word Ustasha mottos. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustasha slogans, for example the use of the letter U which was worn by a special unit called Ustashas during World War II on their caps. Next came the chequerboard with no other insignia which was also a sign of the Independent State of Croatia from the Second World War as well as the glorification of certain Ustasha leaders such as Ante Pavelic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also talked about slogans that were used. You mentioned lines from some songs. What were the slogans, the specific slogans that were used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, as follows: We do not want the Serb militia of Priest Djuic. The next was: We do not want any Serbian spawn in Croatia. The next one was: Serbs back across the Drina. This is a Croatian state. It is a historical Croatian state, and there is no room in it for Serbs or Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did these slogans disrupt relations between people and between the different ethnic groups at the time, especially in your area, in Drnis and its surroundings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to depict the situation for you in terms as simple as possible. Most of the Croats refused to use this sort of language and all these slogans. They even denounced it. But most Serbs, if not all Serbs, were afraid. Groups were formed, people started joining forces, and opinions were exchanged as to what they should do next. That's how it looked at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You talked about these political pre-election rallies, and you said that members of a political party taking part in these elections were there, the HDZ. You even say that one of these rallies was attended by the party president himself, Franjo Tudjman. I think you mentioned the location as the Miljevac plateau. Were the representatives of this party present at these rallies publicly in opposition to these slogans and to the behaviour of the crowds? Did they express their opposition publicly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aside from the top leadership, the lower-ranking officials of the party would drive people on to madness. They were infected by rage, madness and hatred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you speak about what was happening at all these pre-election rallies, can you tell us how you obtained this information? How do you know about all of these things that you've now shared with us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the line of duty that I learned about this because I was in charge of security for these rallies, most of them, if not actually all. They were announced, there was a legal obligation to announce such rallies, and I was in charge of police security at these.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that mean that it was the police that provided security at these rallies in order to uphold law and order? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you name an example of how these slogans and speeches that were held affected those present? Do you have any personal insight into that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly. The village of Gradac, Drnis municipality, I don't know which month, spring, possibly early summer, I was at a rally with massive amounts of people in attendance, 5.000 or 6.000 people, and where I come from that's quite a crowd. I went there with some police officers to provide security. When I arrived in that village, and a lot of people there know me because I had worked in the area for quite a long time, so people came to greet me. Many of them invited me to share a drink. Their intentions were pure as driven snow. However, after the rally, and I'm not sure who that person is called who was in charge of the rally, no one spoke to me again, no one called me again, no one invited me to share drinks with them. Something extremely unpleasant happened to me. There was a man walking on crutches, he approached me. He raised a crutch and hit me over the head. As a result, my cap fell on the ground. All this was filmed by a Croatian TV crew in a bid to show how badly the Serb police were behaving. I went to the president of the municipality, who was in one of the adjacent houses, and I told him about what was going on. Or, rather, I asked him what it was that was going on. After that no one spoke to me again. Even before all of this, at the very beginning of this rally I noticed a group of people, elderly people, more serious people you might say, who were saying, this is no place nor us, "Let's all just up sticks and go home." Croatian people. Elderly people, ethnic Croats, but serious people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that mean that the pre-election rallies themselves directly affected the behaviour of the population? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain about that. That was the main vehicle for the propagation of fear and hatred, I'm quite certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this might be a convenient time to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, we are sorry you've just started, but this is the time we knock off. We will have to come back on Monday. The Court will adjourn to Monday, the 28th of August, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of August, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
